questions.s: W: Where do you work?
questions.e: "At" introduces a workplace; the adjective comes before the noun. The full reply is: "I work at a small bakery downtown."

questions.s: M: What time did you wake up?
questions.e: Past simple with a clock time: "at six thirty". The full reply is: "I woke up at six thirty this morning."

questions.s: W: Is there a laundry room in your building?
questions.e: "There is" plus a place phrase. The full reply is: "Yes, there is one in the basement."

questions.s: M: What does Sofia want to be?
questions.e: Simple present with "she" needs -s. The full reply is: "She wants to become a nurse like her mother." "want" is wrong after "she"; the verb needs "wants".

questions.s: W: Does this train stop at Central Station?
questions.e: "Need" is followed by "to" plus the base verb. The full reply is: "No, you need to take the next one."

questions.s: M: How many classes do you have today?
questions.e: "Only" goes before the main verb. The full reply is: "I only have two classes this afternoon."

questions.s: W: What is your favorite season?
questions.e: "Because" is followed by a full clause. The full reply is: "I like summer best because the days are very long."

questions.s: M: Where should we meet?
questions.e: "Let's" is followed by the base verb with no "to". The full reply is: "Let's meet in front of the library." "to meet" is extra: "Let's to meet" is ungrammatical.

questions.s: W: Why is Hamza so happy?
questions.e: Past simple tells what happened. The full reply is: "He got a good grade on his test." "gets" is present tense and does not match a finished event.

questions.s: M: Do you want to order pizza?
questions.e: "Would rather" is followed by the base verb with no "to". The full reply is: "I would rather cook something at home." "to cook" is extra: "would rather to cook" is ungrammatical.

questions.s: M: Is the lab open on weekends?
questions.e: The adverb "only" can go before "open" or after it, and both orders are natural. The full reply is: "I believe it is open only on Saturdays."

questions.s: W: Which movie did you see?
questions.e: A relative clause ends with the preposition "about". The full reply is: "It was the one that everyone has been talking about."

questions.s: M: Can I pay by card?
questions.e: "Have to" is followed by the base verb. The full reply is: "Yes, but you have to spend at least ten dollars." "must to" is extra; "must" never takes "to".

questions.s: W: Will the shuttle run during the holiday?
questions.e: "Will" is followed by the base verb. The full reply is: "I heard that it will run less often during the holiday." "runs" is extra: after "will" the verb must stay in the base form.

questions.s: M: I heard you are moving.
questions.e: "Closer" is the comparative of "close". The full reply is: "Yes, I found an apartment that is closer to campus." "more close" is the wrong comparative form.

questions.s: W: Did Kwame explain why he was absent?
questions.e: "Had to" expresses a past obligation; "told us" is followed by "that". The full reply is: "He told us that he had to see a doctor."

questions.s: M: What is the plan for tonight?
questions.e: "Either ... or" joins two options in parallel form. The full reply is: "We could either cook at home or go out." "neither" needs "nor", not "or".

questions.s: W: I can't believe the test is tomorrow.
questions.e: "Wish" plus the past form talks about an unreal present. The full reply is: "I know. I wish we had more time to prepare." "have" is wrong after "wish"; the past form "had" is needed.

questions.s: M: Where did you get such a nice bike?
questions.e: A "when" clause gives the time and comes after the main clause. The full reply is: "My uncle gave it to me when I graduated."

questions.s: W: The trail looks steep.
questions.e: "Worth" is followed by a noun phrase. The full reply is: "It is, but the view is worth the climb."

questions.s: W: Why did the experiment fail?
questions.e: After "not only" at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion): "was the equipment", not "the equipment was". The full reply is: "Not only was the equipment faulty but the samples were also contaminated."

questions.s: M: Did the committee approve the budget?
questions.e: After "only after ..." at the start, the main clause uses question order: "did they approve". The full reply is: "Only after the figures had been revised did they approve it." "approved" is extra because "did" already carries the past tense.

questions.s: W: Is it too late to change my registration?
questions.e: Third conditional: "if" plus past perfect, then "could have" plus the past participle. The full reply is: "If you had asked last week, you could have changed it."

questions.s: M: Who designed this building?
questions.e: "Whose" shows possession in a relative clause. The full reply is: "It was designed by an architect whose earlier buildings I had always admired." "who" does not show possession, so it cannot replace "whose".
questions.pf: It was designed by an architect

questions.s: W: Will the company hire more staff?
questions.e: "Unless" means "if not", so the main clause is negative or modal and no second negative is needed. The full reply is: "Unless sales improve soon, the company cannot afford new staff."

questions.s: M: What did you think of the lecture?
questions.e: "So" plus an adjective plus "that" shows result. The full reply is: "I found it so fascinating that I forgot to take notes." "such" is used before a noun phrase ("such a fascinating talk"), not directly before an adjective.

questions.s: W: Do you know who is responsible for the schedule?
questions.e: In an embedded question the subject question word "who" is followed directly by the verb. The full reply is: "I'm not sure, but I can find out who is in charge." "does" is extra: embedded questions do not use do-support.

questions.s: M: Why was the trip postponed?
questions.e: Passive with an infinitive: "was expected to get worse". The full reply is: "It was postponed because the weather was expected to get worse."

questions.s: W: Did Chen help you with the poster?
questions.e: "Could not have" plus the past participle shows something that would not have happened. The full reply is: "He did, and I could not have finished it without him."

questions.s: M: What does the author mean by the title?
questions.e: Adverb of frequency before the main verb; "more ... than" is a comparison. The full reply is: "The title suggests that knowledge often raises more questions than it answers." "that" is extra because the clause already follows "suggests that".

questions.s: M: Where did you buy that backpack?
questions.e: Simple past statement with place phrases. Full sentence: "I bought it from a shop near the station." The extra chunk "in" does not belong: a second preposition cannot be added before "a shop".

questions.s: W: Is your English class big?
questions.e: "There are" + quantity + noun + place phrase. Full sentence: "No, there are only twelve students in the class."

questions.s: W: Do you want some coffee?
questions.e: Negative present simple: "do not" + base verb. Full sentence: "No, thanks. I do not drink coffee at night." The extra chunk "does" does not belong: "does" does not agree with the subject "I".

questions.s: M: How do you get to school?
questions.e: Adverb of frequency "usually" before the main verb. Full sentence: "I usually go to school by bus with my sister."

questions.s: W: Where is my phone?
questions.e: Place phrases: "on the table next to your keys". Full sentence: "It is on the table next to your keys." The extra chunk "in" does not belong: "in the table" is not correct for a surface; "on" is already placed.

questions.s: M: Did you have a good weekend?
questions.e: Simple past with two actions joined by "and". Full sentence: "Yes, I visited my grandparents and cooked dinner." The extra chunk "visit" does not belong: both verbs must be past forms, so "visit" is wrong.

questions.s: W: What are you doing tonight?
questions.e: "be going to" + base verb for plans. Full sentence: "I am going to watch a movie with friends." The extra chunk "watching" does not belong: after "going to" the verb stays in the base form.

questions.s: M: Is your sister a student?
questions.e: Present simple third person: "she studies". Full sentence: "Yes, she studies medicine at a big university." The extra chunk "study" does not belong: "study" does not take the -s ending needed after "she".

questions.s: W: Why are you so tired?
questions.e: Simple past with a time phrase "last night". Full sentence: "I went to bed after midnight last night." The extra chunk "go" does not belong: "go" is the base form and does not match the past time.

questions.s: M: Can I borrow your pen?
questions.e: Modal "can" + base verb. Full sentence: "Sure, you can borrow my pen until Friday." The extra chunk "borrowed" does not belong: after "can" the verb must be the base form.

questions.s: W: How long have you lived here?
questions.e: Present perfect with "since" + a year. Full sentence: "I have lived in this city since 2019." The extra chunk "for" does not belong: "for" needs a length of time, not a year.

questions.s: M: What did the teacher say?
questions.e: Reported speech with backshift: "would be". Full sentence: "She said that the test would be on Thursday." The extra chunk "will be" does not belong: "will be" does not match the past reporting verb "said".

questions.s: W: Is this seat taken?
questions.e: Modal "can" + base verb. Full sentence: "No, you can sit here if you want." The extra chunk "sits" does not belong: after "can" the verb has no -s ending.

questions.s: M: Why did you miss the bus?
questions.e: Past continuous "was talking" for an action in progress. Full sentence: "I missed it because I was talking to my neighbor." The extra chunk "talked" does not belong: "was" must be followed by the -ing form "talking", not a past form.

questions.s: W: Which bag is yours?
questions.e: Noun phrase with a place phrase as subject, then "is". Full sentence: "The red one on the chair is mine."

questions.s: M: Are you good at math?
questions.e: Present continuous "am getting" for a gradual change. Full sentence: "Not really, but I am getting better every week." The extra chunk "gets" does not belong: "gets" does not combine with "am".

questions.s: W: How was the trip?
questions.e: Comparative "more expensive than". Full sentence: "It was much more expensive than we planned." The extra chunk "most" does not belong: "most" is a superlative and does not fit with "than".

questions.s: M: Can you work on Saturday?
questions.e: "would like to" + "but" + reason. Full sentence: "I would like to but I have a family dinner." The extra chunk "likes" does not belong: after "would" the verb is "like", with no -s.

questions.s: W: Who is the man talking to Dr. Kim?
questions.e: Relative pronoun "who" for a person. Full sentence: "He is the student who won the science prize." The extra chunk "which" does not belong: "which" is used for things.

questions.s: M: What does the sign say?
questions.e: Future passive-like form "will be closed" in a "that" clause. Full sentence: "It says that the library will be closed on Monday." The extra chunk "was" does not belong: "was" does not combine with "will be".

questions.s: M: I'm writing a report about this course.
questions.e: Embedded question: statement order, no "do". Full sentence: "Can you tell me how many students are enrolled in the course?" The extra chunk "do" does not belong: "do" would turn the embedded question into a direct one.

questions.s: W: When did you realize the mistake?
questions.e: Inversion after "Not until": the auxiliary "did" comes before the subject. Full sentence: "Not until I got home did I notice it." The extra chunk "I noticed" does not belong: "I noticed" would repeat the subject and break the inversion.

questions.s: W: Is the paper going to be reviewed?
questions.e: Passive future: "will be reviewed by". Full sentence: "It will be reviewed by two professors next month." The extra chunk "has" does not belong: "has" does not combine with "will be".

questions.s: M: What did she ask you?
questions.e: Reported yes/no question: "whether" + statement order. Full sentence: "She asked me whether I had finished the survey." The extra chunk "did I" does not belong: "did I" would use question order inside a reported question.

questions.s: W: Why are you so stressed?
questions.e: Mixed conditional: past perfect in the "if" clause, "would" + present result. Full sentence: "If I had started earlier, I would not be so busy now." The extra chunk "will not" does not belong: "will not" does not match the past perfect "had started".

questions.s: M: What did you see on the way home?
questions.e: Participle phrase after a noun: "a student carrying". Full sentence: "I saw a student carrying a huge pile of books." The extra chunk "carried" does not belong: "carried" would give a second finite verb with no subject.

questions.s: M: Is the shuttle worth using?
questions.e: "not only ... but also" pair. Full sentence: "Yes, it not only saves time but also money." The extra chunk "and" does not belong: "and" would replace "but also" and break the pair.

questions.s: W: What should I do with the extra forms?
questions.e: Passive with a modal: "must be returned". Full sentence: "They must be returned to the office by noon." The extra chunk "return" does not belong: a passive needs the participle "returned", not the base form.

questions.s: M: Which candidate impressed the committee most?
questions.e: Possessive relative pronoun "whose". Full sentence: "The candidate whose presentation was the clearest impressed us." The extra chunk "who" does not belong: "who" cannot replace "whose" before the noun "presentation".

questions.s: W: Do you like living in a big city?
questions.e: "wish" + past subjunctive "were". Full sentence: "I wish it were less crowded and noisy." The extra chunk "is" does not belong: "is" does not express an unreal wish.

questions.s: W: What time does the library close?
questions.e: Simple present with a time phrase: the verb comes first, then "at" plus the time. The full reply is: "The library closes at nine o'clock on weekdays."

questions.s: M: Where did you find that great jacket?
questions.e: Past simple followed by prepositional phrases of place. The full reply is: "I bought it at a small shop on Park Street."

questions.s: W: Does Priya live near the campus?
questions.e: Simple present with "she" needs the -s form. The full reply is: "Yes, she lives in a small apartment near the main gate." "live" is the wrong form after "she"; the verb must be "lives".

questions.s: M: What do you usually eat for breakfast?
questions.e: An adverb of frequency goes before the main verb. The full reply is: "I usually eat toast with a cup of tea."

questions.s: W: Are you coming to the study group?
questions.e: Modal "can't" plus the base verb, then "because of" plus a noun. The full reply is: "I can't come because of my lab tonight."

questions.s: W: How can I get to the stadium?
questions.e: Modal "should" plus the base verb "take", followed by a noun phrase and a place phrase. The full reply is: "You should take the green line train from the main station."

questions.s: W: How do you get to school?
questions.e: Simple present with an adverb of frequency; "with" tells who goes along. The full reply is: "I usually take the bus with my brother."

questions.s: M: What is Amara doing now?
questions.e: Present progressive: is plus verb-ing. The full reply is: "She is reading a book in the library now." "reads" cannot follow "is"; the progressive needs "reading".

questions.s: W: Why were you late for class?
questions.e: A because-clause gives the reason and follows the main clause. The full reply is: "I was late because my bus broke down."

questions.s: M: Could you lend me a pen, please?
questions.e: Modal "can" is followed by the base verb with no "to". The full reply is: "Of course, you can borrow it until tomorrow." "to" is extra: "can to borrow" is ungrammatical.

questions.s: W: Where is the nearest pharmacy?
questions.e: "There is" plus place phrases. The full reply is: "There is one next to the post office on Main Street."

questions.s: M: Do you like your new job?
questions.e: The verb "enjoy" is followed by a verb-ing form. The full reply is: "Yes, I enjoy working with my new team."

questions.s: W: What does your sister study?
questions.e: Simple present, third person singular. The full reply is: "She studies biology at a university in Canada." "study" is wrong after "she"; it needs the -s form "studies".

questions.s: M: How often do you go to the gym?
questions.e: A frequency phrase ("three times a week") comes at the end. The full reply is: "I go there three times a week."

questions.s: W: What's the weather like today?
questions.e: An intensifier ("very") comes before the adjective. The full reply is: "I think it is very cold outside today."

questions.s: M: Does the cafeteria serve breakfast?
questions.e: Prepositions of time: "from ... until ...". The full reply is: "Yes, it serves breakfast from seven until ten."

questions.s: W: Can you help me with my homework?
questions.e: Modal "can" plus the base verb, with the time phrase last. The full reply is: "Sure, I can help you after dinner."

questions.s: M: What did you buy at the market?
questions.e: Past simple needs "bought"; adjectives come before the noun. The full reply is: "I bought some fresh vegetables for dinner." "buy" is the base form and does not show the past tense.

questions.s: W: Which seat is yours?
questions.e: The pattern "the one next to ..." identifies a thing by its position. The full reply is: "Mine is the one next to the window."

questions.s: M: Where is the bookstore?
questions.e: "Across from" is a fixed prepositional phrase of place. The full reply is: "It is across from the student center."

questions.s: W: Are your parents coming to the graduation?
questions.e: Present progressive for a plan; the place phrase comes last. The full reply is: "Yes, they are flying here from another city."

questions.s: M: Do you play any sports?
questions.e: Simple present with a short list of details; the time phrase is last. The full reply is: "I play basketball with friends on Sundays."

questions.s: W: What's wrong with your laptop?
questions.e: Past simple with "went" plus an adjective; "during" plus a noun phrase. The full reply is: "The screen suddenly went black during my presentation."

questions.s: M: How do I get to the gym?
questions.e: An imperative starts with the base verb and gives directions in order. The full reply is: "Go straight down this hall and turn left."

questions.s: W: What are you reading?
questions.e: "About" introduces the topic; the adjective comes before the noun. The full reply is: "It is a book about a young doctor and her family."

questions.s: M: Is it okay if I sit here?
questions.e: Passive voice: is plus past participle, then "by" for the doer. The full reply is: "Sorry, this seat is taken by my friend." "take" is the base form; the passive needs "taken".

questions.s: W: How was the exam?
questions.e: A comparative adjective with "than" compares two things. The full reply is: "It was much easier than I expected." "more" cannot be added before "easier" because the comparative is already formed.

questions.s: M: What does Yuki do on weekends?
questions.e: An adverb of frequency comes before the main verb, which takes -s after "she". The full reply is: "She often goes hiking with her friends." "go" is wrong after "she"; the verb must be "goes".

questions.s: W: Who is your favorite teacher?
questions.e: A because-clause gives the reason; the adverb comes after the object. The full reply is: "My favorite teacher is Mr. Chen because he explains things clearly."

questions.s: M: Why did you move to a new apartment?
questions.e: "Too" plus an adjective means more than is acceptable. The full reply is: "The old one was too noisy for me." "enough" follows an adjective and would not fit before "noisy" or give this meaning.

questions.s: W: Where can I buy a train ticket?
questions.e: Modal "can" plus a base verb, then a place phrase. The full reply is: "You can buy one at the ticket office downstairs."

questions.s: M: Why is the cafeteria so crowded?
questions.e: Present perfect with "just" between the auxiliary and the past participle. The full reply is: "Because a big class has just ended."

questions.s: W: Is that your backpack on the floor?
questions.e: Simple present with "it" needs -s; "belongs to" shows ownership. The full reply is: "No, it belongs to a student from my class." "belong" is wrong after "it"; it needs "belongs".

questions.s: M: How long is the movie?
questions.e: "About" comes before the number in an approximate length. The full reply is: "It lasts about two hours and ten minutes."

questions.s: W: Whose notebook is this?
questions.e: A because-clause explains the reason; "is on" shows position. The full reply is: "It is Mateo's because his name is on the cover."

questions.s: M: Do you want some coffee?
questions.e: Negative simple present: "don't" plus the base verb after "I". The full reply is: "No, thanks. I don't drink coffee in the evening." "doesn't" is used with he, she or it, not with "I".

questions.s: W: Where did Kwame go yesterday?
questions.e: Past simple with a because-clause for the reason. The full reply is: "He went to the dentist because his tooth hurt."

questions.s: M: What should I bring to the picnic?
questions.e: Modal "could" plus a base verb offers a suggestion. The full reply is: "You could bring some fruit for everyone."

questions.s: W: Is Olga in the lab?
questions.e: Present progressive: is plus verb-ing. The full reply is: "No, she is working in the library today." "works" cannot follow "is" in a progressive sentence.

questions.s: M: How was your trip to the mountains?
questions.e: "Very" comes before the adjective; "got tired" means became tired. The full reply is: "It was wonderful, but we got very tired on the last day."

questions.s: W: Do you need a pen?
questions.e: The adverb "already" goes before the main verb. The full reply is: "No, I already have one in my bag."

questions.s: M: When does the concert start?
questions.e: Simple present for a schedule: verb, then "at" plus the time. The full reply is: "It starts at seven thirty on Saturday."

questions.s: W: Who is that man talking to the teacher?
questions.e: Possessives come before the noun: "our new student's father". The full reply is: "I think he is our new student's father."

questions.s: M: Do the buses run on Sundays?
questions.e: "Less often than" compares how frequent two things are. The full reply is: "Yes, but they come less often than on weekdays."

questions.s: W: Which button do I press?
questions.e: An imperative with a position phrase: "on the left". The full reply is: "Press the green one on the left."

questions.s: M: Where is the closest ATM?
questions.e: "There is" plus a place phrase. The full reply is: "There is one inside the main building."

questions.s: W: What did you do last night?
questions.e: A because-clause follows the main clause; "very" comes before the adjective. The full reply is: "I stayed home because I was very tired."

questions.s: M: Does Lucas work on campus?
questions.e: Simple present with "he" needs -s. The full reply is: "Yes, he works at the front desk of the library." "work" is the wrong form after "he"; the verb must be "works".

questions.s: W: When is your birthday?
questions.e: Dates use "on", and "the third of March" has a fixed order. The full reply is: "My birthday is on the third of March."

questions.s: M: Why are you studying so hard?
questions.e: "Next week" is a fixed time phrase at the end. The full reply is: "I have a big exam next week."

questions.s: W: What is in the box?
questions.e: Adjectives come before the noun, and "of" links the photos to the owner. The full reply is: "It has some old photos of my family."

questions.s: M: Would you like to join our team?
questions.e: The adverb "already" comes after the verb "be". The full reply is: "Thanks, but I am already on another team."

questions.s: W: How much is the monthly bus pass?
questions.e: "Costs" is followed by the price, then "for" plus the group. The full reply is: "I think it costs forty dollars for students."

questions.s: M: Where did you park your car?
questions.e: Past simple followed by a place phrase. The full reply is: "I parked it behind the science building."

questions.s: W: Is the museum free?
questions.e: "But" joins two clauses that contrast. The full reply is: "It is free for students but adults pay ten dollars."

questions.s: M: What happened to your phone?
questions.e: Past simple needs the -ed form. The full reply is: "I dropped it on the stairs yesterday." "drop" is the base form and does not show the past.

questions.s: W: Do your classes start early?
questions.e: "Only one class" is singular, so the verb takes -s. The full reply is: "Only one class starts before nine o'clock."

questions.s: M: What kind of music do you like?
questions.e: Adjective order: opinion adjective, then the noun phrase; "when" begins a time clause. The full reply is: "I like quiet piano music when I study."

questions.s: W: What is your new roommate like?
questions.e: "But" shows contrast; "a bit" softens the adjective. The full reply is: "He is very friendly but a bit messy."

questions.s: M: What did the sign say?
questions.e: Reported speech shifts "will" to "would". The full reply is: "It said that the road would be closed for repairs." "will" does not fit because the sentence reports a past statement.

questions.s: M: I'm looking for the language lab.
questions.e: An indirect question keeps statement word order: "where the lab is", not "where is the lab". The full reply is: "Do you know where the language lab is?" "does" is extra because an indirect question needs no auxiliary.

questions.s: W: I'm new here and I'm a little lost.
questions.e: After "tell me how", use statement order: subject "I" before "can". The full reply is: "Could you tell me how I can get to the gym?" "do" is extra: an indirect question does not take do-support.

questions.s: M: Has Lucas finished his thesis?
questions.e: Present perfect: "has" plus the past participle, with "just" between them. The full reply is: "Yes, he has just submitted it to his advisor." "have" does not agree with "he"; the auxiliary must be "has".

questions.s: W: Have you ever been to the art museum downtown?
questions.e: Present perfect with "never" between "have" and the participle. The full reply is: "No, I have never visited any museums here." "ever" is extra because "never" already makes the sentence negative.

questions.s: M: Why is Aisha upset?
questions.e: Present perfect continuous: "has been waiting" for an action that continues up to now. The full reply is: "She has been waiting for an answer since Monday."

questions.s: W: Where is the book I lent you?
questions.e: Present perfect negative with "yet" at the end; "finish" is followed by verb-ing. The full reply is: "I'm sorry, but I haven't finished reading it yet." "didn't" does not fit with "yet" and the past participle.

questions.s: M: Which professor do you recommend?
questions.e: A relative clause with "who" describes a person. The full reply is: "Dr. Gupta is the professor who teaches the introductory course." "which" is used for things, not people.

questions.s: W: I can't find my keys anywhere.
questions.e: A relative clause after a noun: "the jacket that you wore yesterday". The full reply is: "Did you check the jacket that you wore yesterday?" "who" refers to people, not to a jacket.

questions.s: M: Is there anything I should know before the exam?
questions.e: A contact relative clause ("the chapters we covered") needs no relative pronoun; "definitely" goes before the main verb. The full reply is: "You should definitely review the chapters we covered in class."

questions.s: W: Do you think the library will be open on Sunday?
questions.e: Modal "can" plus a base verb offers help. The full reply is: "I'm not sure, but I can check the website for you."

questions.s: M: How long has Priya lived in this city?
questions.e: "Since" introduces the starting point of a period; "for" is used with a length of time. The full reply is: "She has lived here since she was a child." "for" is extra: "for she was a child" is ungrammatical.

questions.s: W: What did the professor say about the deadline?
questions.e: Reported speech with a modal: "must" plus the base verb. The full reply is: "She said that we must submit our papers by Friday."

questions.s: M: I'm thinking of taking a photography class.
questions.e: A yes/no indirect question uses "if" and statement order. The full reply is: "Good idea. I wonder if the college offers a course this semester." "does" is extra because the embedded question has no auxiliary.

questions.s: W: Can I ask you something about the project?
questions.e: Question word order: question word, auxiliary, subject, main verb. The full reply is: "Of course. What would you like to know?" "do" is extra: the question already has the auxiliary "would".

questions.s: M: This coffee shop is always full.
questions.e: A relative clause with "where" describes a place. The full reply is: "It is the only place where students can study until midnight."

questions.s: W: The bus is late again.
questions.e: After "wish", use "would" for something we want to change. The full reply is: "I wish they would run more buses." "will" is not used after "wish"; the wish form is "would".

questions.s: M: Did you hear that Mateo got the internship?
questions.e: Passive voice: "was chosen" shows what happened to Mateo. The full reply is: "Yes, I heard he was chosen from two hundred applicants."

questions.s: W: Why isn't the projector working?
questions.e: Present perfect: "has" plus the past participle. The full reply is: "I think someone has unplugged it by mistake."

questions.s: M: How do I submit my application?
questions.e: "Before" introduces a time clause with subject and verb. The full reply is: "You have to upload your documents before you click submit."

questions.s: W: Is the new café any good?
questions.e: A superlative takes the present perfect, and "ever" goes between "have" and the participle. The full reply is: "It is the best café that I have ever visited."

questions.s: M: What was the lecture about?
questions.e: An embedded question uses statement order with no auxiliary. The full reply is: "The professor explained why some animals sleep all winter." "do" is extra: "why do some animals sleep" is a direct question.

questions.s: W: Are you free to meet tomorrow?
questions.e: Future negative with "won't" plus "be able to". The full reply is: "I'm afraid I won't be able to meet until Thursday."

questions.s: M: Where did Chen leave the keys?
questions.e: An embedded question keeps statement order and drops "did". The full reply is: "I don't remember where he put them." "did" is extra because "where he put them" is not a direct question.

questions.s: W: How are you getting to the airport?
questions.e: "Offer" is followed by "to" plus the base verb. The full reply is: "My roommate has offered to drive me there."

questions.s: M: Why was the class canceled?
questions.e: A because-clause gives the reason after the main clause. The full reply is: "The professor couldn't come because she was sick."

questions.s: W: I'm not sure which course to take.
questions.e: "Whichever" means any one that; it begins a noun clause. The full reply is: "You should take whichever one fits your schedule best." "which" does not join with "one" to mean "any one that".

questions.s: M: Do you know anyone in the chemistry department?
questions.e: A relative clause with "who" describes a person. The full reply is: "Yes, my cousin is a student who works in the lab."

questions.s: M: Is it true that you switched from economics to history?
questions.e: "Interested" is followed by "in"; "more" comes before the adjective. The full reply is: "I realized that I was more interested in history."

questions.s: M: Does Sofia still play the violin?
questions.e: Present perfect negative with "since" plus a past time. The full reply is: "She has not played it since last year." "never" is extra because "not" already makes the sentence negative.

questions.s: W: Where are the extra chairs?
questions.e: A relative clause with "that" describes a place. The full reply is: "They are in the closet that is next to the stage."

questions.s: M: Can you recommend a good restaurant?
questions.e: A relative clause with "where" describes the place. The full reply is: "I recommend the place where we had lunch last week."

questions.s: W: Why didn't you answer my message?
questions.e: "Realize" can be followed by a "that" clause with normal statement order. The full reply is: "I didn't realize that my phone was on silent."

questions.s: M: What's the matter with Olga?
questions.e: A contact relative clause ends with a preposition: "the scholarship she applied for". The full reply is: "She didn't get the scholarship she applied for." "who" is wrong because the clause refers to a thing, not a person.

questions.s: W: Have you decided where to go for the trip?
questions.e: "Still" goes after "are" and before the main verb. The full reply is: "Not yet. We are still deciding which city to visit."

questions.s: M: Is that the professor you were telling me about?
questions.e: A relative clause with "who" describes a person. The full reply is: "Yes, she is the one who won the teaching award last year."

questions.s: W: Do you mind if I open the window?
questions.e: Present progressive "is getting" describes a change; "a little" softens the adjective. The full reply is: "Not at all. It is getting a little warm in here."

questions.s: M: Where is your brother these days?
questions.e: Present perfect with a result in the present; "for" gives the reason. The full reply is: "He has moved to another city for a new job."

questions.s: W: What is the museum known for?
questions.e: A possessive adjective must match the singular subject "it". The full reply is: "It is famous for its collection of ancient coins." "their" is plural and does not match "it".

questions.s: M: Could you open the door for me?
questions.e: "Because" introduces the reason and is followed by a full clause. The full reply is: "Sorry, I can't right now because my hands are full."

questions.s: W: Why were you at the library so long?
questions.e: A relative clause with "that" describes a thing. The full reply is: "I was looking for a book that I needed for my essay."

questions.s: M: Why weren't you at the study group yesterday?
questions.e: Modal-like "had to" + base verb, then object and time phrase. Full sentence: "I had to finish my lab report before noon." The extra chunk "finishing" does not belong: "had to" must be followed by the base verb, not the -ing form.

questions.s: W: Where is the registrar's office?
questions.e: Statement word order in a reply (subject, verb, place phrase); no inversion. Full sentence: "I think the registrar's office is next to the main library."

questions.s: M: How long have you been learning Spanish?
questions.e: Present perfect continuous with "since" + a starting point. Full sentence: "I have been studying it since last September." The extra chunk "for" does not belong: "for" goes with a length of time, so it cannot introduce "last September".

questions.s: W: Do you like your new apartment?
questions.e: Comparative with "than": "much bigger than". Full sentence: "Yes, it is much bigger than my old one." The extra chunk "more" does not belong: "more bigger" would be a double comparative.

questions.s: M: Does the cafeteria open early?
questions.e: Frequency adverb between the subject and the main verb. Full sentence: "Yes, it usually opens before seven on weekdays." The extra chunk "is" does not belong: "is" would give the ungrammatical "it is opens".

questions.s: W: Where should I put these books?
questions.e: Imperative with the pronoun object before the place phrases. Full sentence: "Please put them on the shelf behind the door."

questions.s: M: Is the library open on Sundays?
questions.e: "Only" comes before the word it limits. Full sentence: "No, it is only open from Monday to Saturday." The extra chunk "opened" does not belong: "is opened" changes the meaning and the grammar; the adjective "open" is needed.

questions.s: W: Did you finish the assignment?
questions.e: Future with "will" + base verb after "but". Full sentence: "Not yet, but I will finish it tonight." The extra chunk "am" does not belong: "am" cannot be combined with "will".

questions.s: M: Why is the lab so crowded today?
questions.e: "has to" + base verb "submit". Full sentence: "Because everyone has to submit a report by Friday." The extra chunk "submitting" does not belong: "has to" cannot be followed by the -ing form.

questions.s: W: What was the art museum like?
questions.e: Comparative "more interesting than". Full sentence: "It was much more interesting than I expected." The extra chunk "most" does not belong: "most" is a superlative and does not fit with "than".

questions.s: M: Can you help me move this desk?
questions.e: "too" + adjective + "for" + noun phrase. Full sentence: "Sure, but it looks too heavy for one person."

questions.s: W: When will the results be posted?
questions.e: Passive future "will be posted". Full sentence: "They will be posted on the website next week." The extra chunk "are" does not belong: "are" cannot be added before "will be".

questions.s: M: Have you met the new librarian yet?
questions.e: Simple past with a finished time phrase "last week". Full sentence: "Yes, I met her at the front desk last week." The extra chunk "have" does not belong: "have met" does not go with "last week".

questions.s: W: Why did you take the bus today?
questions.e: Present continuous passive "is being repaired". Full sentence: "My car is being repaired this week." The extra chunk "repairing" does not belong: the passive needs the past participle "repaired", not "repairing".

questions.s: M: Which professor teaches chemistry this term?
questions.e: Relative clause "who teaches chemistry" after the noun it describes. Full sentence: "The professor who teaches chemistry is Dr. Patel."

questions.s: W: Do you know where the bookstore is?
questions.e: Place expression "across from" followed by a noun phrase. Full sentence: "I think it is across from the student center."

questions.s: M: What are you doing this weekend?
questions.e: "be going to" + base verb for plans. Full sentence: "I am going to visit my cousin in Chicago." The extra chunk "visiting" does not belong: after "going to" the verb must be the base form "visit", not "visiting".

questions.s: W: Why did the class end early?
questions.e: Past continuous "was feeling" + adjective. Full sentence: "The professor was feeling sick this morning." The extra chunk "did" does not belong: "did" cannot be combined with "was feeling".

questions.s: M: Which bus goes to the airport?
questions.e: Modal "should" + base verb. Full sentence: "You should take the number twelve bus." The extra chunk "taking" does not belong: after "should" the verb must be the base form "take", not "taking".

questions.s: W: How was your interview?
questions.e: Comparative "better than" with a past perfect clause. Full sentence: "It went better than I had hoped." The extra chunk "best" does not belong: "best" is a superlative and cannot be followed by "than".

questions.s: M: Could you lend me your notes?
questions.e: "finish" is followed by a gerund (writing). Full sentence: "Of course, but I haven't finished writing them." The extra chunk "write" does not belong: after "finished" the verb must be the -ing form, not "write".

questions.s: W: What did the manager say about the schedule?
questions.e: Reported speech with backshift: "would change". Full sentence: "He said that the shifts would change next month." The extra chunk "will" does not belong: "will change" does not match the past tense "said".

questions.s: M: Are you coming to the party tonight?
questions.e: "would like to" + "but" + reason clause. Full sentence: "I would like to but I have an exam tomorrow."

questions.s: W: Where did you leave your umbrella?
questions.e: Preposition "in" is used with a taxi (a car). Full sentence: "I think I left it in the taxi." The extra chunk "on" does not belong: "on" is wrong with "the taxi".

questions.s: M: Why is she so tired?
questions.e: Present perfect continuous with "since" + a starting point. Full sentence: "She has been working two jobs since January." The extra chunk "for" does not belong: "for" needs a length of time, not "January".

questions.s: W: Is there anything I can do to help?
questions.e: Imperative with an object and a destination "to the office". Full sentence: "Yes, please carry these boxes to the office."

questions.s: M: How often do you visit your parents?
questions.e: "try to" + base verb, with "almost" before "every weekend". Full sentence: "I try to visit them almost every weekend."

questions.s: W: What do you think of the new course?
questions.e: Comparative with a degree phrase: "a little harder than". Full sentence: "I think it is a little harder than I expected." The extra chunk "hardest" does not belong: "hardest" is a superlative and cannot take "than".

questions.s: M: Who is the tall woman by the door?
questions.e: Relative pronoun "who" for a person. Full sentence: "She is the person who gave the talk yesterday." The extra chunk "which" does not belong: "which" is used for things, not for a person.

questions.s: W: Did you hear the news about the lab?
questions.e: Reported content in a "that" clause with the passive "will be closed". Full sentence: "Yes, I heard that it will be closed for repairs."

questions.s: W: Did the professor give us any homework?
questions.e: "ask someone to + base verb". Full sentence: "Yes, she asked us to read chapter four." The extra chunk "reading" does not belong: after "to" the base verb "read" is needed, not "reading".

questions.s: M: Why do you always sit in the front row?
questions.e: Modal "can" + base verb, with "better there" at the end. Full sentence: "I can hear the lecture better there." The extra chunk "could" does not belong: "could" would change the meaning to a past or polite possibility.

questions.s: W: What happened to your bike?
questions.e: Active past tense with a subject "someone". Full sentence: "Someone stole it from the parking lot." The extra chunk "was stolen" does not belong: "was stolen" is passive and cannot follow "someone" as the agent.

questions.s: M: How did you get here so fast?
questions.e: Verb + object + prepositional phrase of path. Full sentence: "I took a shortcut through the park."

questions.s: W: Are you going to apply for the scholarship?
questions.e: "think about" + gerund. Full sentence: "I am thinking about applying for it next month." The extra chunk "to apply" does not belong: a preposition like "about" must be followed by the -ing form, not "to apply".

questions.s: M: Is the exam going to be difficult?
questions.e: Equality comparison "as hard as". Full sentence: "I don't think it will be as hard as the last one." The extra chunk "than" does not belong: "than" is for unequal comparisons and cannot replace the second "as".

questions.s: W: Who told you about the concert?
questions.e: Verb + indirect object + "about" phrase. Full sentence: "My roommate told me about it yesterday."

questions.s: M: Where can I buy a used textbook?
questions.e: Modal "can" + base verb. Full sentence: "You can find one at the campus bookstore." The extra chunk "finding" does not belong: after "can" the verb must be the base form "find".

questions.s: W: Why is the printer not working?
questions.e: Present perfect "has run out of" + noun. Full sentence: "It has run out of paper again."

questions.s: M: What do you usually do after class?
questions.e: Frequency adverb "often" before the main verb. Full sentence: "I often go to the gym with my friends." The extra chunk "goes" does not belong: the subject "I" takes the base form "go", not "goes".

questions.s: M: I'd like to join the photography club.
questions.e: Embedded question: statement word order after the question word "when". Full sentence: "Could you tell me when the next meeting will be held?" The extra chunk "does" does not belong: "does" would turn the embedded question into a direct question.

questions.s: W: Where can I get the housing application form?
questions.e: Passive with a modal: "can be downloaded". Full sentence: "The form can be downloaded from the housing page." The extra chunk "downloading" does not belong: a passive needs the past participle "downloaded", not "downloading".

questions.s: M: Is the new dormitory any good?
questions.e: Correlative pair "not only ... but also" joining two comparatives. Full sentence: "Yes, it is not only cheaper but also closer to campus." The extra chunk "and" does not belong: "and" would replace "but also" and break the pair.

questions.s: W: Does the professor ever cancel class?
questions.e: Inversion after the negative adverb "rarely": auxiliary before subject. Full sentence: "Rarely does she cancel a lecture without warning." The extra chunk "cancels" does not belong: after the auxiliary "does" the main verb stays in the base form, so "cancels" is wrong.

questions.s: M: Have you ever been late to Dr. Lee's class?
questions.e: Inversion after "never" with the present perfect. Full sentence: "Never have I arrived after the lecture began." The extra chunk "arrive" does not belong: after "have" the participle "arrived" is needed, not the base form "arrive".

questions.s: W: What did the advisor tell you?
questions.e: Reported speech: "told me that" + clause. Full sentence: "She told me that I should register before the deadline." The extra chunk "to" does not belong: "to" cannot be placed between "that" and the clause subject.

questions.s: M: Why didn't you take the earlier bus?
questions.e: Third conditional: "if + past perfect, would have + participle". Full sentence: "If I had known about the delay, I would have left much earlier." The extra chunk "will have" does not belong: "will have" does not match the past perfect "had known".
questions.pf: If I had known about the delay,

questions.s: W: Where did you meet your study partner?
questions.e: Participle phrase after "while": "while waiting". Full sentence: "I met her while waiting for the shuttle at the north gate." The extra chunk "wait" does not belong: after "while" a reduced clause takes the -ing form, not "wait".

questions.s: M: What kind of job are you looking for?
questions.e: Complex noun phrase with a relative clause: "a position that offers". Full sentence: "I want a position that offers flexible hours and good pay." The extra chunk "offer" does not belong: the verb must agree with the singular noun "position": "offers".

questions.s: W: Which topics will be on the midterm?
questions.e: Embedded question with statement word order. Full sentence: "I don't know which topics the professor will include on the midterm." The extra chunk "will she" does not belong: "will she" would reverse the order inside the clause.

questions.s: M: Has the final grade been posted?
questions.e: Passive with a modal: "should be posted". Full sentence: "Not yet, but it should be posted by tomorrow noon." The extra chunk "should have" does not belong: "should have" needs a participle and would give a past meaning.

questions.s: W: How can I improve my writing?
questions.e: "by" + gerund to show a method. Full sentence: "You could improve it by reading more academic articles." The extra chunk "read" does not belong: after the preposition "by" the verb takes the -ing form.

questions.s: M: Why was the lecture hall so noisy?
questions.e: Reduced relative clause "working next door" modifying "the builders". Full sentence: "Because the builders working next door were using heavy machinery." The extra chunk "was using" does not belong: the plural subject "the builders" needs "were", not "was".

questions.s: W: Did you enjoy the documentary?
questions.e: Concession with "although" + comparative. Full sentence: "I did, although it was longer than I expected."

questions.s: M: Do you think the tuition will go up?
questions.e: "doubt" + clause with a future form. Full sentence: "I doubt the university will raise tuition this year." The extra chunk "raising" does not belong: after the subject "the university" the modal "will" needs the base verb "raise".

questions.s: W: Why is the library so crowded tonight?
questions.e: Relative clause "who have exams next week" modifying the subject. Full sentence: "Because the students who have exams next week are studying there." The extra chunk "is studying" does not belong: the plural subject "the students" needs "are studying".

questions.s: M: Could you explain why the experiment failed?
questions.e: Passive in a "because" clause: "was not controlled". Full sentence: "I think it failed because the temperature was not controlled." The extra chunk "did" does not belong: "did" cannot be used with the passive "was not controlled".

questions.s: M: What are the lab rules?
questions.e: Passive with a modal: "must be worn". Full sentence: "Safety goggles must be worn at all times in the lab." The extra chunk "wear" does not belong: a passive needs the past participle "worn", not the base form "wear".

questions.s: M: What is special about the new dorm?
questions.e: Inversion after "Not only": "is it quiet", then "but ... also". Full sentence: "Not only is it quiet but it is also cheap." The extra chunk "does it" does not belong: "does it" cannot be followed by the adjective "quiet" without a main verb.

questions.s: M: I heard you got accepted into the program!
questions.e: Passive reporting verb "was told that" with backshift "would receive". Full sentence: "Yes, and I was told that I would receive a scholarship." The extra chunk "will receive" does not belong: "will receive" does not match the past form "was told".

questions.s: W: Where do you want to study abroad?
questions.e: Relative adverb "where" for a place. Full sentence: "I would like to study in a country where English is widely spoken." The extra chunk "which" does not belong: "which" would need a preposition ("in which") and no longer fits the chunks.
questions.pf: I would like to study in a country

questions.s: M: Did you submit the application on time?
questions.e: "wish" + past perfect for a regret about the past. Full sentence: "I did, but I wish I had checked it more carefully." The extra chunk "have" does not belong: "have" cannot replace the auxiliary "had" after the subject "I".

questions.s: W: What was the main reason for the delay?
questions.e: Passive with an agent: "was caused by". Full sentence: "The delay was caused by a shortage of qualified staff." The extra chunk "caused" does not belong: "caused" alone is active and cannot follow "was caused" in the same verb phrase.

questions.s: M: Have you finished the report yet?
questions.e: Third conditional: "would have finished ... if ... had not broken down". Full sentence: "I would have finished it already if the printer had not broken down." The extra chunk "did not" does not belong: "did not" does not match the past perfect needed in the "if" clause.
questions.pf: I would have finished it already

questions.s: W: Can you recommend a good place to study?
questions.e: "adjective + enough" word order. Full sentence: "The reading room on the third floor is quiet enough to study in." The extra chunk "enough quiet" does not belong: "enough" follows the adjective: "quiet enough".

questions.s: M: How did the students react to the news?
questions.e: Past perfect passive in a "that" clause after "surprised". Full sentence: "Most of them seemed surprised that the exam had been postponed." The extra chunk "has been" does not belong: "has been" does not fit the past time of "seemed".

questions.s: W: Why did you change your major?
questions.e: "after" + gerund. Full sentence: "I changed it after realizing that I enjoyed biology more than chemistry." The extra chunk "realized" does not belong: after the preposition "after" the verb takes the -ing form.

questions.s: M: Has anyone seen my laptop?
questions.e: Relative clause "that looked like yours" directly after the noun it describes. Full sentence: "I saw a laptop that looked like yours near the printer."

questions.s: W: What would you do if you had more free time?
questions.e: Second conditional: "if + past, would + base verb". Full sentence: "If I had more free time, I would spend more time on my hobbies." The extra chunk "will" does not belong: "will" does not match the past form "had" in the "if" clause.
questions.pf: If I had more free time,

questions.s: M: Where is the meeting going to take place?
questions.e: Present perfect passive "has been moved". Full sentence: "It has been moved to the room next to the cafeteria." The extra chunk "moving" does not belong: a passive needs the participle "moved", not "moving".

questions.s: W: I need to talk to someone about my schedule.
questions.e: Embedded question with "who" as subject: "who is responsible". Full sentence: "Could you tell me who is responsible for course registration?"

questions.s: M: I'd like to rent a locker.
questions.e: Embedded question: statement order, so no "does" before the subject. Full sentence: "Could you let me know how much a locker costs for a semester?" The extra chunk "does" does not belong: "does" is needed only in a direct question ("How much does a locker cost?").

questions.s: M: Should we have lunch at the dining hall on Friday?
questions.e: "wonder if" introduces an embedded yes/no question, with statement word order. Full sentence: "I was wondering if it would be open that day."

questions.s: M: Why did the department move the seminar?
questions.e: Past continuous passive: "was being renovated". Full sentence: "It was moved because the usual room was being renovated."

questions.s: W: Did you finish the project before the deadline?
questions.e: Inversion with "No sooner ... than": the auxiliary "had" comes before the subject. Full sentence: "No sooner had I submitted it than the system crashed." The extra chunk "have" does not belong: "have" does not match the past narrative.

questions.s: M: Was the concert crowded?
questions.e: Inversion after "Hardly": "had the doors opened". Full sentence: "Hardly had the doors opened when people rushed in." The extra chunk "have" does not belong: "have" is the wrong tense for a past event.

questions.s: W: Why did the experiment succeed this time?
questions.e: Comparative correlative "The more ..., the better ...". Full sentence: "The more carefully we measured the better the results were." The extra chunk "did we" does not belong: "did we" would turn the clause into a question.

questions.s: M: Is the new software difficult to learn?
questions.e: "so + adjective + that" for a result. Full sentence: "It is so complicated that most users need training." The extra chunk "such" does not belong: "such" needs a noun phrase, not an adjective alone.

questions.s: W: Is it too late to register for the workshop?
questions.e: Subjunctive after "essential that": the base verb for every subject. Full sentence: "It is essential that you sign up by Friday." The extra chunk "signs up" does not belong: "signs up" has an -s ending, which the subjunctive does not use.

questions.s: M: Who organized the career fair?
questions.e: Cleft sentence "It was ... that ...". Full sentence: "It was the student council that organized the whole event." The extra chunk "which" does not belong: "which" is not used after a cleft with a group of people.

questions.s: W: What did the dean announce yesterday?
questions.e: Reported speech with backshift: "would remain". Full sentence: "He announced that the library would remain open until midnight." The extra chunk "will remain" does not belong: "will remain" does not match the past reporting verb "announced".

questions.s: M: Why isn't Maria here?
questions.e: Present perfect with "since" + a starting point. Full sentence: "She is unable to attend because she has been ill since Monday." The extra chunk "for" does not belong: "for" needs a length of time, not "Monday".
questions.pf: She is unable to attend because she

questions.s: W: Did the committee approve the plan?
questions.e: "despite the fact that" + clause. Full sentence: "It did, despite the fact that several members objected." The extra chunk "although" does not belong: "although" cannot be combined with "despite" in the same phrase.

questions.s: M: Which classes should I take next semester?
questions.e: "whichever" + noun as a free relative clause. Full sentence: "You should take whichever courses are required for your major."

questions.s: W: How did you find out about the scholarship?
questions.e: Passive with an agent and a relative clause. Full sentence: "I was told about it by the professor who taught me last spring."
questions.pf: I was told about it by

questions.s: W: Do you know where the new science building is?
questions.e: Reduced description with a past participle: "is located behind". Full sentence: "It is located behind the gym that was built last year." The extra chunk "locate" does not belong: "is locate" is wrong; the passive-like "is located" needs the participle.

questions.s: M: What was the main idea of the lecture?
questions.e: "argue that" + clause with a passive modal "should be designed". Full sentence: "The professor argued that cities should be designed for pedestrians rather than cars." The extra chunk "designing" does not belong: a passive needs the past participle "designed", not "designing".

questions.s: W: Why do you want to work abroad?
questions.e: Gerund subject + "would" + base verb. Full sentence: "Working abroad would give me the chance to meet people from other cultures." The extra chunk "gave" does not belong: after "would" the base form "give" is needed, not a past form.
ck: to meet people from other cultures

questions.s: M: Did the lab results surprise you?
questions.e: Past perfect negative: "had not expected". Full sentence: "They did, since I had not expected a difference." The extra chunk "did not" does not belong: "did not" would give a simple past that does not fit the earlier time.

questions.s: W: What happens if I miss the deadline?
questions.e: "unless" means "if not": the paper is refused without an extension. Full sentence: "Your paper will not be accepted unless you get an extension." The extra chunk "if" does not belong: "if" would make the sentence say the paper is refused when you get an extension, which is illogical.

questions.s: M: How come you were late?
questions.e: Inverted third conditional: "had + subject + not + participle" replaces "if". Full sentence: "I would have been on time had the train not been delayed." The extra chunk "if" does not belong: "if" cannot be used together with the inversion "had the train".
questions.pf: I would have been on time

questions.s: W: Is the printer working now?
questions.e: Present perfect passive negative: "has not been repaired". Full sentence: "I'm afraid it has not been repaired yet." The extra chunk "have not" does not belong: "have not" does not agree with the singular subject "it".

questions.s: M: Which of these two apartments do you prefer?
questions.e: Relative clause "that is closer to the campus" after "the one". Full sentence: "I prefer the one that is closer to the campus." The extra chunk "what" does not belong: "what" cannot follow a noun phrase like "the one".

questions.s: W: Why didn't the experiment work?
questions.e: Modal perfect passive: "might have been contaminated". Full sentence: "It might have been contaminated by dust in the lab." The extra chunk "has been" does not belong: "has been" cannot follow the modal "might".

questions.s: In our education course, we are discussing the transition from high school to university. In some countries, it is common for students to take a gap year, a year away from formal study to work, travel or volunteer before starting university. Supporters say it helps students mature and choose the right field. Critics say it delays students' careers and that many never return to study. Would you recommend that students take a gap year before university? Why or why not?
questions.e: I would recommend a gap year, as Noor does, but for an additional reason: it teaches independence. Many students go straight from living with their parents to living in a university dormitory, where meals, schedules and support services are all organized for them. A student who has spent a year working in a cafe or volunteering in another city learns to manage money, solve problems alone and deal with adults in a professional way. These skills make the first year of university much less stressful, and students who feel confident are more likely to stay in their program. Patrick's concern about forgetting math is reasonable, but students can avoid it by taking a short online course or reviewing for a few weeks before classes begin. One year is a small part of a long career, and the maturity gained during that year can make the rest of a student's education more successful.

ps.text: I wouldn't recommend it. After a year away, it is hard to get back into the habit of studying, and students may forget a lot of what they learned in school, especially in subjects like math. They also start earning a full salary a year later than their classmates.

questions.s: This week in business, we are studying entrepreneurship. People who start a new company face many early decisions, and one of the most important is whether to start alone or with one or more co-founders. Working alone means full control, while a partner brings extra skills, money and support but also the possibility of disagreement. If you were starting a small business, such as an online clothing shop or a cafe, would you rather start it alone or with a partner? Explain your choice.
questions.e: Ahmed's worry about disagreements is understandable, but I would still start a business with a partner, as Camila suggests. One reason that has not been mentioned is that a partner helps you see your own mistakes. When you work alone, nobody questions your ideas, so it is easy to become too excited about a plan that will not work. For example, if I wanted to open a cafe in a quiet street because the rent is cheap, a partner might point out that very few customers would ever walk past it. A second opinion like this can prevent expensive errors in the early months, when a small business has very little money to lose. To reduce the risk of conflict, partners should agree in writing from the beginning how decisions will be made and what will happen if one of them wants to leave. With clear rules, a partnership offers far more benefits than problems.

If my partner is skilled in the areas where I am weak, the business has a much better chance. We could also share the stress during difficult months.

ps.name: Ahmed
ps.text: I would rather start alone. Partners often disagree about important things, like how fast to grow or how to spend profits, and these arguments can destroy both the business and the friendship. When I am the only owner, I can make quick decisions and keep all the profits for myself.

questions.s: Our sociology class is studying volunteering and civic participation. Some high schools require students to complete a certain number of volunteer hours, for example forty hours at a hospital, library or community center, before they can graduate. Supporters say this teaches responsibility and connects young people with their communities. Others argue that volunteering loses its meaning when it is forced. Do you think high schools should require volunteer work for graduation? Explain your view.
questions.e: I agree with Lucia that high schools should require volunteer work, and I would add that it helps students explore possible careers. A teenager who volunteers at a hospital may discover a strong interest in nursing, while another who helps at a library might realize they enjoy teaching children to read. These experiences are difficult to get any other way at that age, because most employers will not hire students without experience. Volunteering also gives students something real to write about in university applications and to discuss in job interviews. Kai raises an important point about students who already work, so I think schools should be flexible. For instance, they could reduce the required hours for students with family responsibilities or allow them to volunteer during school holidays. With this flexibility, the requirement would open doors for young people without being unfair to anyone.

questions.s: In environmental science, we are studying the urban heat island effect. Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside because roads and buildings absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Two common solutions are planting many more trees along streets and covering roofs with light-colored materials that reflect sunlight. If a city wanted to reduce summer heat and had money for only one of these solutions, which should it choose? Explain why.
questions.e: Wei makes a good point about how quickly reflective roofs work, but I would choose trees, like Emma. One benefit she did not mention is that trees help with heavy rain as well as heat. Their roots and the soil around them absorb water, so streets flood less during summer storms. In many cities, hot summers and sudden storms happen together, so one investment can solve two problems. Trees also last for decades, while roof coatings slowly get dirty and lose their ability to reflect sunlight unless they are cleaned or replaced. It is true that young trees need time to grow, but the city could start with fast-growing species in the hottest neighborhoods and plant more each year. In the long run, trees provide shade, cleaner air and better protection from flooding, which makes them more valuable than reflective roofs.

They also clean the air and make neighborhoods more beautiful. A reflective roof might cool a building, but it does nothing for someone waiting at a bus stop in the sun.

ps.name: Wei
ps.text: Reflective roofs are the better choice. Trees take many years to grow large enough to give real shade, and they need water and care. Reflective roofs work from the first day. They also lower the temperature inside buildings, so people use less air conditioning, which saves money and electricity.

questions.s: In urban planning, we have been examining how cities use their historic centers. Several cities have started closing the central streets to cars on weekends, turning them into spaces for walking, cycling, markets and street performances. Some residents love the change, while others complain that it makes it harder to reach the center, especially for older people. Would you support closing your city center to cars every weekend? Explain why or why not.
questions.e: I would support closing the city center to cars on weekends, as Tomas does, and I would add a benefit related to history and culture. Many city centers contain old buildings, fountains and small squares that people hardly notice when they are busy watching for traffic. On a car-free weekend, residents and tourists can slow down, look around and learn about their city's past. Museums and guides could even offer free walking tours on those days. In addition, less traffic means less pollution, which helps protect old stone buildings from damage over time. Ayesha's concern about older people and those with disabilities is very important, but it can be solved. The city could run free electric shuttles from parking areas at the edge of the center and allow special permits for people who need a car. With these services, everyone could enjoy a calmer, more attractive city center.

questions.s: In technology and society, we are looking at how digital tools are changing the way students read. Many universities now offer digital textbooks, which are often cheaper and can be read on a laptop, tablet or phone. However, some students still prefer printed books and say they understand and remember more when they read on paper. For university courses, do you think digital textbooks or printed textbooks are the better choice for students? Explain your answer.
questions.e: Julia lists some real advantages, but I agree with Bilal that printed textbooks are the better choice for university courses. Besides the problem of distractions, there is the issue of eye strain. University students already spend many hours a day looking at screens for online assignments, emails and lectures. Adding long reading sessions on a laptop can cause headaches and tired eyes, which makes it harder to concentrate in the evening. Reading on paper gives the eyes a break. Printed books can also be shared or sold to next year's students, while many digital textbooks expire after one semester and cannot be passed on to anyone. This means the price difference is often smaller than it first appears. For short articles or quick searches, digital texts are convenient, but for the main textbook that students must study carefully all semester, paper is still the more effective option.

questions.s: Our psychology unit this week is about attention and learning. Many students listen to music while they study, and they say it helps them relax and stay focused. However, some researchers believe that music, especially songs with lyrics, competes with the brain's ability to process new information. Based on your own experience and knowledge, do you think listening to music while studying helps students or makes their studying less effective? Explain why.
questions.e: In my opinion, whether music helps depends on the type of studying, but for most serious learning I agree with Musa that it makes studying less effective. One point that has not been mentioned is the difference between studying and taking the exam. If students always review with music playing, the room will feel very different during the test, which happens in complete silence. Some people find it harder to remember information in a setting that does not match the one where they learned it. Practicing in quiet conditions prepares them better for the real exam. That said, Adriana's experience is valid for certain tasks. Music without lyrics can make repetitive work, such as organizing notes or copying formulas, more pleasant. So my advice would be to turn the music off when reading or memorizing new material and to save it for the simpler parts of studying.

questions.s: In public health, we have been studying sleep, which affects memory, mood and physical health. Surveys show that many teenagers sleep far less than the eight to ten hours experts recommend. Some schools have responded by starting classes later in the morning. Others focus on educating families, for example by encouraging parents to keep phones and tablets out of bedrooms at night. Which approach do you think would do more to help teenagers get enough sleep, and why?
questions.e: I agree with Sara that starting school later would do more to help teenagers sleep, and I would add a practical reason. A later start time is one decision made by the school, and it affects every student at once. Educating families, on the other hand, depends on thousands of separate homes. Some parents will follow the advice, but others work night shifts, are too busy to check, or simply do not agree, so the results would be very uneven. A schedule change also helps with travel. In many areas, students catch a bus before seven o'clock, which means waking up extremely early even if they went to bed on time. Liam is right that phones keep teenagers awake, and schools could still teach good sleep habits in health classes. But a policy that reaches everyone automatically is more likely to make a real difference than advice that families may ignore.

questions.s: In media studies, we are examining how young people follow current events. A growing number of people under twenty-five now get most of their news from short videos lasting one or two minutes. Others still prefer longer articles from newspapers or news websites. Each format has strengths and weaknesses. Which do you think is a better way for young people to stay informed about the world: short news videos or longer written articles? Explain your choice.
questions.e: Jae is right that videos are quick and easy to understand, but I agree with Clara that longer articles are a better way to stay informed. Another reason is that articles make it easier to check where information comes from. A good article names its sources, quotes experts and often links to original reports, so readers can confirm the facts for themselves. Short videos, in contrast, are frequently copied and shared by accounts that nobody knows, and it can be very difficult to tell whether the clip is recent, complete or even real. For example, an old video of a flood might be shared as if it happened yesterday. Reading articles also improves young people's vocabulary and concentration, which helps them in their studies. Short videos can be a useful way to discover a story, but young people should then read a full article to understand it properly.

questions.s: In our economics course, we have been looking at the competition between small local shops and large chain stores. In many towns, family-owned bookshops, bakeries and hardware stores have closed because they cannot match the low prices of national chains and online retailers. Some towns now offer small businesses lower rent or tax reductions to help them survive. Do you think towns should use public money to support small local shops? Why or why not?
questions.e: I agree with Hassan that towns should support small local shops, and I want to add an economic argument. When people spend money at a family-owned business, much more of that money stays in the town. The owner lives locally, hires local workers and often buys supplies from other nearby businesses, such as a bakery that buys flour from a regional mill. A large chain, by contrast, sends much of its profit to headquarters in another city. Supporting local shops therefore helps other businesses and jobs in the same town. Mia makes a reasonable point that taxpayers' money is limited, so I think the support should be modest and temporary. For example, a town could reduce rent on empty shop spaces for a new business's first two years. This gives small shops a fair chance to establish themselves without creating permanent costs for taxpayers.

questions.s: This week we are looking at how university courses are organized and what helps students succeed. Many universities record their lectures and post them online, so students can watch them at any time. Some instructors worry that this encourages students to skip class, while others think attendance should simply be a personal choice for adults. What do you think? Should universities require students to attend lectures in person, or should attendance be optional when recordings are available? Explain why.
questions.e: I understand Mateo's point about students with jobs, but I still believe universities should require attendance for most lectures. My main reason is that learning at a university is not only about receiving information; it is also about learning from classmates. In a live lecture, students hear the questions that other people ask, and these questions often reveal problems they had not noticed themselves. Recordings rarely capture this, because the microphone usually picks up only the professor. In addition, attending class builds a routine. When I have a fixed time for a course each week, I keep up with the readings, whereas recordings make it very easy to postpone everything until the night before the exam. That said, universities could allow a small number of absences each term for students with work or family duties. This would keep the benefits of attendance while remaining fair to people in difficult situations.

questions.s: In our unit on workplace management, we have been discussing new ways of organizing working time. Several companies have tested a four-day work week, in which employees work four longer days or four normal days with no loss of pay. Supporters say it improves productivity and well-being, but critics argue that it does not suit every type of business. In your opinion, would a four-day work week be good for most companies and their employees? Why or why not?
questions.e: Sofia makes a good point about hospitals and shops, but I believe a four-day week would still be good for most companies, as long as it is introduced flexibly. One benefit that has not been mentioned is hiring. Today, many skilled workers can choose between several employers, and a shorter week is a very attractive benefit that costs less than a large salary increase. A company that offers it can attract talented people and keep them longer, which saves a great deal of money on recruiting and training new staff. Furthermore, businesses that need to stay open every day do not have to close for a day. They can schedule employees on different days, so the shop is always staffed while each person still works four days. Of course, every company should test the idea for a few months first and measure the results before making it permanent.

questions.s: Our sociology course has been examining what makes a neighborhood feel like a real community. Researchers have found that people who know their neighbors tend to feel safer and more satisfied with where they live. However, in many modern cities, residents hardly speak to the people next door. Which do you think does more to build a sense of community in a neighborhood: shared physical spaces, such as parks and community gardens, or organized events, such as street festivals and clubs? Explain your choice.
questions.e: Both Amara and Lucas raise good points, but I agree with Amara that shared spaces do more to build community. My reason is that spaces include people who would never sign up for an event. Shy residents, elderly people living alone, or newcomers who do not speak the local language well may feel uncomfortable at a festival full of strangers. A community garden, however, lets them join slowly. They can water their own plants, nod to the person at the next plot, and gradually start talking when they feel ready. Over time, these small, repeated contacts create trust, which is the foundation of any community. Events are still useful, but I think they work best when they take place in a shared space. For example, a garden could host a harvest day once a year, so the event strengthens relationships that the space has already started.
